name: Tata Duende
description: Tata Duende is one of Belize's most famous mythical creatures — a powerful forest spirit that protects animals and the jungle. Described as a small, bearded man about three feet tall who wears a wide-brimmed red hat, animal skins for clothing, and has his feet pointing backwards. He notably lacks thumbs. Parents warn children never to show Tata Duende their thumbs, or he will break or bite them off. He is known for whistling to mimic his victims, braiding horses' manes, and luring children deeper into the forest. However, among the Yucatec Maya of Belize, he is also known as Nukuch Tat and is seen as a good guardian spirit who protects children in the bush. Offerings are still given to him for protection and help before entering the forest In Belize folklore, this figure is known among the Maya and Creole people.
source: Belizean oral tradition; snip Wikipedia; snip Folktales America; snip GrisDismation Legends of Belize

name: Tautramunken
description: Tautramunken (the Monk of Tautra) is a ghostly figure that haunts the ruins of Tautra Cistercian monastery on the island of Tautra in the Trondheimsfjord, near Frosta. The monastery was founded in 1207 and was one of the most important Cistercian houses in Norway until it was dissolved during the Reformation in 1532. The ghost is believed to be a monk who refused to leave the monastery when it was closed, or who was killed during the dissolution. The specter appears as a white-robed Cistercian monk walking the ruins at twilight, particularly on misty evenings. Local tradition says the monk can be seen kneeling in prayer where the monastery church once stood. Tautra is also known for its unique natural beauty and bird life, and the ghost legend is an integral part of the island's cultural heritage
source: Norwegian folklore; the Monk of Tautra is a documented spectral apparition in Trøndelag history.

name: Teryel
description: Teryel is the most famous ogress in Kabyle (Algerian Amazigh) mythology — a terrifying female monster with an anthropophagic (man-eating) appetite. According to a foundational Kabyle myth, when humanity was created as fifty men and fifty women, 98 chose to settle and build houses, but one man and one woman chose to live in the wild. The man became a lion (izem) and the woman became Teryel, the first ogress. Teryel represents the untamed, wild feminine that rejects domesticity and social norms. In Kabyle folklore, she lives isolated in caves and wilderness, eating her own children when hungry and devouring anyone who approaches her domain. Despite her monstrous nature, Teryel is also a figure of resistance — she rejects patriarchal society's rules, making her both feared and respected. She is the antithesis of the domesticated Kabyle woman: independent, powerful, and utterly free. Her daughter Lunja plays the role of the beautiful captive in her cave, creating a complex mother-daughter dynamic in Kabyle oral tradition
source: Frobenius, Kabyle folk tales (1921); Lacoste-Dujardin; Henri Basset; Kabyle oral traditions; Amazigh Wiki

name: Three-Fingered Jack (Jamaican Outlaw Hero)
description: Three-Fingered Jack (Jack Mansong or Jack Mantong) was a legendary Jamaican outlaw and folk hero who terrorized the island in the late 18th century (c. A former slave from the western parish of Westmoreland, Jack escaped into the rugged Cockpit Country and formed a band of runaway slaves who robbed plantations, freed enslaved people, and resisted British colonial authority. His name derived from a distinctive physical feature -- he had only three fingers on one hand. Jack became a Robin Hood-like figure in Jamaican folklore, celebrated for his cunning, supernatural invulnerability, and defiance of the colonial system. He was believed to possess an obeah charm that made him bulletproof and gave him the ability to disappear into the forest. After a long campaign of terror, Jack was eventually hunted down and killed by Maroon trackers led by Quashee (or Quashie), but his legend only grew after death. His story was romanticized in 18th-century English ballads, plays, and novels, making him one of the first Caribbean folk heroes to achieve international fame
source: Jamaican oral tradition, Jamaica folklore

name: Thủy Tinh (Water Spirit)
description: Thủy Tinh (literally 'Water Spirit' or 'Water God') is the powerful deity of waters, seas, and floods in Vietnamese mythology. In the famous legend from the Hùng King period, Thủy Tinh sought to marry the beautiful princess Mỵ Nương but lost to his rival Sơn Tinh (Mountain Spirit), who arrived first with wedding gifts. Enraged by jealousy and humiliation, Thủy Tinh summoned storms, raised the waters, and unleashed floods against the mountains to destroy Sơn Tinh and reclaim the princess. However, Sơn Tinh raised the mountains higher each time. Their eternal conflict continues annually — Thủy Tinh's floods represent the devastating monsoon rains that inundate Vietnam's Red River Delta each year. Though defeated each season, Thủy Tinh never gives up, symbolizing both the destructive power of nature and the inexorable cycle of Vietnamese geography. The myth reflects the ancient Vietnamese struggle to tame their flood-prone landscape through dikes and water management
source: Vietnamese folk religion — Thủy Tinh water god.

name: Tilberi
description: Tilberi (also Snakkur) is a worm-like magical creature created by women in Icelandic witchcraft traditions to steal milk from neighbors' cows. The tilberi was made from a stolen dead man's rib and grey wool, hidden between the woman's breasts and fed with stolen communion wine for three Sundays. Once created, it was sent to suckle from the woman's inner thigh, creating a wart-like mark where it fed. The tilberi would then be sent to neighbors' farms where it stretched its worm-like body to reach both teats of a cow simultaneously, drinking all the milk. It returned to its creator's dairy window crying Full magi, mamma! (Full belly, Mama!) and vomited the milk into her churn. The tilberi could be destroyed by ordering it to count lamb droppings into three piles — the number three was magical and would cause it to burst. The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery and Witchcraft in Hólmavík features the tilberi prominently
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Tin Hinan
description: Tin Hinan is the legendary ancestral queen of the Tuareg people, one of the most revered figures in Algerian and broader Saharan folklore. According to legend, Tin Hinan was a noblewoman who traveled from the Tafilalt oasis in the Atlas Mountains, leading her people across the Sahara to settle in the Hoggar Mountains of southern Algeria. Her arrival marked the beginning of the Tuareg civilization in the central Sahara. She is credited with laying the foundations for Tuareg cultural identity, including their unique matrilineal traditions, alphabet (Tifinagh), and social structures. In 1925, a 4th-century CE tomb of a wealthy woman was discovered at Abalessa in the Hoggar, which Tuareg tradition identifies as Tin Hinan's burial place. The skeleton was found with gold jewelry, Roman artifacts, and a funerary couch — evidence of her high status and the far-reaching trade networks of the ancient Sahara. Tin Hinan represents leadership, resilience, and the power of women in Saharan societies. Her legend is a founding myth for the Tuareg nation
source: Archaeological findings at Abalessa; oral Tuareg traditions; CRASC Dictionary of Algerian Myths; Ibn Khaldun references

name: Tislit n'Anzar
description: Tislit n'Anzar (the Bride of Anzar) is a mythological figure from Amazigh (Berber) folklore practiced in Tunisia and across the Maghreb. She is associated with an ancient rain-calling ritual known as Taghonja or Tagnja performed during times of drought. In the myth, Anzar is the god of rain who falls in love with a mortal woman. When she refuses him, Anzar withholds rain from the land, causing drought and suffering until the woman relents and agrees to marry him — at which point life-giving rain returns. The ritual involves creating a wooden doll shaped from a ladle or pestle (called Taghonja), dressing it in bridal clothes as Tislit, and parading it through villages while women chant prayers for rain. The doll is sprayed with water, and a ritual feast is held near a river or shrine. This ancient practice, still performed in parts of southern Tunisia (particularly Djerba and Tataouine) and Algeria, represents one of the oldest continuously practiced rain-making rituals in the Mediterranean world
source: Folk Culture Bahrain (rain ritual study); Laoust, Mots et choses berbères; Genevois, Kabyle texts; PASRI climate research

name: Trickster Scorpion
description: The Trickster Scorpion is a popular figure in Mauritanian folklore, embodying the dangers and deceptions of the desert. In one of the best-known tales, 'The Trickster Scorpion and the Desert Spirits,' a clever scorpion outwits both humans and supernatural beings through a combination of cunning, diplomacy, and strategic use of its venomous sting. The story spread across Mauritania as parents told it to their children and travelers carried it across the sands. The trickster scorpion is not purely evil but is opportunistic and survival-focused, reflecting the harsh realities of Saharan life where one must be clever to survive. Unlike the purely malicious scorpion of reality, the trickster scorpion in folklore is endowed with speech, complex reasoning, and a moral complexity that makes it a compelling character. The tales serve as both entertainment and practical education, teaching children about the real dangers of scorpions in the desert while also imparting wisdom about dealing with difficult people and situations
source: folktales.africa

name: Trollkatt
description: Trollkatt (troll cat) is a magical cat-like creature in Norwegian folklore, particularly associated with witches and trolls in Vestlandet. The trollkatt can be either a gift from trolls to humans who helped them, or a familiar sent by witches to do their bidding. In Vestlandet tradition, the trollkatt is a large, coal-black cat with glowing green or red eyes. It brings either great luck or terrible misfortune depending on how it is treated. A trollkatt that is well-fed and respected will protect the farm from other supernatural beings and even increase the milk yield of cows. A mistreated trollkatt will spoil food, strangle chickens, and cause nightmares. Witches could send their trollkatt to steal milk from neighbors' cows. The only way to stop a witch's trollkatt was to strike it with a silver button or say specific prayers. Trollkatter were believed to be extremely long-lived and fiercely loyal to their owners
source: Norwegian folklore; the Troll Cat is a magical entity in regional folk tales.

name: Trollkjerringene på Letnesberget
description: Trollkjerringene på Letnesberget (the Troll Witches of Letnesberget) is a legend from the Fosen area of Trøndelag, documented in Birger Sivertsen's collection 'Eventyr og sagn fra Trøndelag'. The story tells of a group of trollkjerringer (female trolls/witches) who lived in the Letnesberget mountain on the Fosen peninsula. These troll witches were known for gathering on the mountain top to hold sabbats, where they would brew magic potions, cast spells on fishing boats, and dance under the full moon. They could control the weather, particularly the storms that batter the Fosen coast, and were blamed for shipwrecks and lost fishing seasons. Local farmers learned to leave offerings at the base of Letnesberget to avoid the troll witches' wrath. The legend is firmly anchored in the Fosen landscape and represents a local version of the widespread trollkjerring tradition
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Trollkona
description: Trollkona (Troll Woman) is the Faroese female troll — a distinct figure in the islands' folklore appearing in legends tied to specific locations across the archipelago. On Skuvoy island, troll women were said to haunt the mountain pastures, stealing sheep and terrorizing shepherds who stayed in the mountain huts at night. The most famous trollkona legend connects her to the very geography of the islands: the island of Koltur is said to be the head of a sleeping troll woman, her body stretching beneath the sea toward Hestur. Near Sandavágur, the Trøllkonufingur (Witch's Finger) rock pillar is the petrified finger of a troll woman caught at dawn while reaching. Multiple versions of the trollkona legend appear in the Færøsk Anthologi collection, each tied to a specific village or island's landscape. The trollkona is the female counterpart to the male giant (risin) and shares the fate of petrification at dawn In Faroe Islands folklore, this figure is known among the Faroe Islands people.
source: Faroese folklore; female trolls in the islands' unique traditions.

name: The Trung Sisters (Hai Bà Trưng)
description: The Trung Sisters — Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị — are Vietnam's most celebrated legendary heroines who led a rebellion against Chinese Han occupation in 40-43 CE. Daughters of a Lạc lord in Mê Linh, they were educated in martial arts and military strategy by their father. When Trưng Trắc's husband Thi Sách was executed by Han officials for plotting rebellion, the sisters raised an army of over 80,000 soldiers, many of them women led by female generals. They stormed 65 Chinese-held citadels, expelled the Han occupiers, and established an independent kingdom with Trưng Trắc as queen — a reign that lasted three years. When the Han Emperor dispatched General Ma Yuan with a massive invasion force, the sisters faced defeat. Rather than be captured, they drowned themselves in the Hát Giang River. Their sacrifice transformed them into national martyrs. Today, temples throughout Vietnam honor them as embodiments of Vietnamese resistance and the indomitable spirit of Vietnamese womanhood
source: Vietnamese historical chronicles (Đại Việt sử ký), Chinese Han dynasty records

name: Tusse
description: Tusse (also Tuss) is a regional variant of the troll/vätte complex found in Halland Småland and Västergötland — a transitional figure between the larger trolls and the smaller vättar. The tusse is smaller than a full troll but larger than a vätte typically described as a shaggy humanoid figure with a tail who lives under large stones or in forest caves. Tussen are tricksters who take pleasure in leading travelers astray moving trail markers and hiding objects. Unlike the genuinely malevolent Puke the tusse is more mischievous than evil. If a traveler gets lost in a Halland forest locals would say 'tussen har lett honom vilse' (the tusse has led him astray). Like the tomte the tusse could be helpful if given offerings of porridge. In Västergötland farmers would leave a bowl of porridge under a large stone on the property known as a tusse-sten (tusse stone). If the porridge was eaten the tusse would protect the farm. If it remained untouched the tusse was offended and trouble would follow. The word 'tusse' survives most clearly in Swedish place names. The tusse represents the intermediate zone in Swedish folklore between the human-scale supernatural (tomtar vättar) and the monstrous (troll giants). The name may derive from Old Norse þurs meaning giant or ogre showing its ancient roots in the language
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Tussehesten
description: Tussehesten (the tusse horse) is a supernatural horse owned by the underjordiske (tusser) in Setesdal folklore. The tusser kept their own horses, which were far superior to human horses — faster, stronger, and more beautiful. On certain nights, the tusse horses could be seen grazing in mountain pastures or running across the valley. A human who could catch and ride a tussehest would have the fastest horse in the valley. However, riding a tussehest was dangerous — if the rider did not treat it properly, the horse would carry them into a mountainside, into the tusse realm, where they would be trapped forever. The tussehest could also be borrowed if one left an offering for the tusser. The tradition appears in Johannes Skar's Gamalt or Setesdal and is related to the more widely known hestenøkken but distinct — the tussehest is not malicious by nature, simply a creature of the hidden folk that can be dangerous if mishandled
source: Norwegian folklore; the Tusse-horse is part of the Underjordiske traditions.

name: Tussepresten
description: Tussepresten (the tusse priest) is a unique figure in Setesdal folklore — the priest of the underjordiske (tusser/hidden people). According to Setesdal tradition, the tusser were not purely pagan but had their own Christian-like religion with their own priest who held rival church services in the valley. The Tusseprest competed with the human priest of Valle church for the souls of the valley. If the human priest rang the church bells too early or too late, the Tusseprest would steal the prayers of the congregation. The Tusseprest held services inside mountains, where the tusser worshipped. Humans who accidentally wandered into a tusse church service would find themselves trapped in an alternative world where time moved differently. The Tusseprest tradition is unique to Setesdal among Norwegian regions — in other parts of Norway, the underjordiske were considered purely pagan. This reflects Setesdal's distinctive theological folk belief where the hidden people were partially Christianized
source: Norwegian folklore; the Tusse Priest is a specific figure in Setesdal folklore.

name: Tzitzimimeh
description: AZTEC STAR DEMONS — terrifying skeletal female deities who were enemies of the sun itself, poised to descend from the heavens and devour humanity during solar eclipses. In Aztec cosmology, the Tzitzimimeh were star spirits associated with darkness, infertility, and the chaotic forces that threatened cosmic order. They were led by the goddess Tlaitecuhtli (or sometimes Citlalicue) and were particularly feared during solar eclipses, when it was believed the demons would descend to earth to consume humans — especially children. Pregnant women were at particular risk, as the Tzitzimimeh were said to transform unborn children into monstrous beings. To ward them off, the Aztecs performed elaborate rituals, including human sacrifice, during eclipses. The arrival of Hernán Cortés and the Spanish conquistadors was interpreted by some as the fulfillment of Tzitzimimeh prophecies — the end of the Fifth Sun. In contemporary Mexican and Mexican-American folklore, Tzitzimimeh survive as a powerful metaphor for apocalypse and existential dread, sometimes appearing in Chicano art and literature as symbols of cosmic destruction and rebirth
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Kintu
description: Kintu is the foundational mythological figure and first human in the oral traditions of the Baganda people of Buganda, Uganda. According to legend, Kintu was the only man on Earth, wandering alone with his cow until Nambi, daughter of the sky god Ggulu, descended from heaven via a rainbow and fell in love with him. After proving himself through a series of trials set by Ggulu—including identifying his cow among a vast herd and eating a massive meal without drinking—Kintu won Nambi's hand in marriage. The couple descended to Earth with gifts of agriculture, including millet and banana cultivation, enabling humanity to thrive. However, they were warned not to return to heaven for any forgotten item. When Nambi sent her brother Walumbe (Death) back for grain, he followed them to Earth, claiming their firstborn and establishing mortality as an inescapable force. Kintu's story explains the Baganda origin, the advent of death, and the foundations of agrarian life
source: Wikipedia - Ugandan folklore, Kintu, Nambi (mythology); Grokipedia; Folklore.earth; Mythlok

name: Nambi
description: Nambi is the daughter of Ggulu (also known as Mugulu), the sky god in Baganda mythology, and becomes the wife of Kintu, the first man. She plays a crucial role as the bridge between the celestial and earthly realms. According to the creation myth, Nambi and her younger sister first discovered Kintu wandering alone on Earth with his cow. Fascinated by this first human, Nambi approached him and later insisted they return to her father in heaven together. After Kintu passed Ggulu's trials, Nambi married him and descended to Earth, bringing essential gifts of agriculture including millet and banana cultivation. She is revered as the mother of all people and associated with fertility and the earth. However, her decision to send her brother Walumbe back to retrieve forgotten grain from heaven allowed death to enter the human world. Nambi embodies both the nurturing force that enables human civilization and the human error that introduced mortality
source: Wikipedia - Nambi (mythology), Ugandan folklore; Folklore.earth - Baganda; Grokipedia - Kintu

name: Walumbe
description: Walumbe is the personification of death in Baganda mythology, the brother of Nambi and son of the sky god Ggulu. In the creation myth, Walumbe is forbidden by his father from knowing about Kintu—the first man—and his sister Nambi's marriage. When Kintu and Nambi prepared to descend to Earth, Ggulu warned them to leave immediately without returning for anything forgotten. But Walumbe tricked them, causing Nambi to forget grain for their journey. When Nambi sent Walumbe back to retrieve it, he followed them to Earth, claiming their firstborn child and establishing death as a permanent part of human existence. Kintu attempted to expel Walumbe but failed, and death became inescapable. Walumbe represents the inescapable reality of mortality in Baganda cosmology. He is often depicted as relentless, cunning, and insatiable, always seeking new souls to claim
source: Wikipedia - Ugandan folklore, List of African deities; Folklore.earth - Baganda; Grokipedia - Kintu

name: Ulda
description: The Ulda (also called Gufihtar, from Old Norse gud vätte 'good underground being') are a mythical race of underground people in Sami folklore. They live inside fells and beneath the earth in a parallel world called Saivo. They are rich, beautiful, well-dressed, and possess all gold and silver under the earth, including hidden treasure. Their reindeer are of exceptional colors and leave no tracks in snow. Tradition says you can claim an Ulda reindeer herd by throwing a metal object over it. They sometimes swap their children for human babies (changelings). If a human eats or drinks in the Ulda world, they must stay forever and become one of them. The Ulda care for the bear in its winter den, feeding it invisibly. They are described as semi-human 'co-dwellers' rather than purely supernatural beings. Some Sami traditions describe them as having foreknowledge of technology — stories tell of humans visiting the Ulda world and seeing radios, telephones, and other inventions long before they existed in the human world
source: beneathnorthernlights.com; saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; Sami Folktales from the Near and Far Worlds

name: Um El Sa'af Wel Leef
aliases: Mother of Palm Leaves and Fiber
description: Um El Sa'af Wel Leef (Mother of Palm Leaves and Fiber) is a tree spirit from Bahraini folklore that dwells behind palm trees in the darkness. Her name references the palm fronds (sa'af) and palm fiber (leef) that are essential materials in traditional Bahraini date palm cultivation. She lurks among the palm groves that once covered much of Bahrain, particularly in rural areas like Muharraq and the villages of the northern island. Parents invoke her name to warn children against wandering into palm plantations alone or staying out after dark near date farms. Like many Bahraini folkloric figures, she serves a utilitarian function — protecting children from the dangers of the agricultural landscape. She represents the animistic belief in spirits inhabiting the natural world and reflects the deep connection between Bahraini culture and the date palm, a symbol of life and sustenance in the arid Gulf environment
source: Gulf Weekly; Zainab Almahdi's 'Um Hmaar Returns!'; oral Bahraini traditions

name: Um Hmaar
description: Um Hmaar (Mother of Donkeys) is a legendary half-woman, half-donkey jinn from Bahraini folklore who preys on children who venture outside at noon. She is described as having the upper body of a woman and the lower body of a donkey, with hooves that make a distinctive sound as she walks through neighborhood streets at midday. Dressed all in black, Um Hmaar knocks on doors while parents take their afternoon naps, begging for food or water. If children open the door, she devours them. Her tell-tale sign is the clopping of her hooves, which sends children fleeing in fear. In some versions, she can transform into a lizard to climb walls and enter homes. The story of Um Hmaar has been adapted into comics and children's books in modern Bahrain, including Zainab Almahdi's illustrated comic 'Um Hmaar Returns!' set in 1960s Bahrain
source: Gulf Weekly; Zainab Almahdi's comics; FolkloreThursday; oral Bahraini traditions

name: Urðarköttur
description: Urðarköttur (Ghoul Cat or Corpse Cat) is a monstrous feline in Icelandic folklore that grows from feral cats or white kittens born with their eyes open. According to tradition, any cat that goes completely feral will eventually become an urðarköttur. White kittens born with their eyes already open sink into the ground immediately after birth and re-emerge after three years as an urðarköttur. The creature grows to the size of an ox, has shaggy white or black fur, and kills indiscriminately. It has a particular taste for corpses and digs up graves in churchyards to eat the dead. Some folklorists believe the Yule Cat (Jólakötturinn) is actually an urðarköttur that became associated with Christmas tradition. The urðarköttur is found in Jón Árnason's folklore collection and represents the deep-seated fear of cats combined with the desecration of graves
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Utlat (Carthaginian Netherworld Spirits)
description: Utlat were spirits of the netherworld in Carthaginian mythology, a tradition that flourished in what is now Tunisia before and during the Roman period. The Carthaginians, descendants of Phoenician settlers, developed a complex religious system that included spirits of the underworld who were both feared and propitiated. These spirits inhabited the realm of the dead and could influence the living world. The Carthaginians believed that the utlat could be contacted through specific rituals involving sacrifice and prayer at the tophet (sacred burial grounds). The most famous tophet in Carthage (in modern Tunis) is the Sanctuary of Tanit, where thousands of urns containing the cremated remains of children and animals were buried as votive offerings. The utlat were particularly associated with Baal Hammon and Tanit, the chief deities of Carthage. Belief in these netherworld spirits reflects the Carthaginian view of death as a continuation of existence in another realm, where the spirits required ongoing attention from the living. The concept of the utlat later blended with Roman ideas of the underworld and, after the Arab conquest, became partially absorbed into Islamic concepts of jinn and spirits of the dead
source: Wikipedia (Punic religion); Carthaginian archaeological sources

name: Vågakallen
description: Vågakallen (the Old Man of Vågan) is the troll king of Lofoten, said to sit on his throne 1,000 meters above sea level in the Lofoten mountains. He was the ruler of the Lofoten trolls and the father of Hestmannen (the Horseman). Vågakallen sat on his mountain throne watching over his kingdom — the Lofoten archipelago, Vestfjorden, and the surrounding sea. According to legend, when he was caught by the sunrise, he and his entire kingdom were turned to stone, becoming the dramatic Lofoten mountains. The Vågakallen rock formation is a famous landmark visible from the sea near Henningsvær. The legend is part of the Helgeland/Lofoten cycle of troll stories that explain the dramatic coastal landscape of Northern Norway. Vågakallen represents the ancient power of the troll kings who ruled the land before humans
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Valravn
description: Valravnen (the Raven of the Slain) is a supernatural raven in Danish medieval ballads and folklore. According to legend, a knight who died unshriven or a person who committed terrible acts could be transformed into a Valravn. The Valravn possesses human intelligence, speaks in human tongues, and has supernatural powers. Its curse can be broken if it drinks the blood of an infant three days old. In Danish ballads (9 versions collected by Svend Grundtvig), the Valravn appears as a talking raven who bargains with humans, demands sacrifices, and reveals secrets. A separate folk tradition holds that if a raven eats the heart of a slain king on the battlefield, it becomes a Valravn with the wisdom and power of the dead king. The Valravn is distinct from the Natravn — it is actively malevolent and intelligent, not merely a damned soul
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Varulv
description: Den danske varulv (the Danish werewolf) has a unique origin not found in other countries: if a pregnant woman crawls through a horse's afterbirth to ease her labor pains, a son will become a werewolf and a daughter will become a mare (nightmare spirit). The Danish varulv is always male and transforms at sunset, his human soul replaced by a wolf's savage nature. Unlike continental werewolves, the Danish varulv does not require a full moon or a wolfskin belt — the curse is carried in the blood from birth. Salvation is uniquely Danish: if the werewolf is cornered and someone says 'Du er ikke varulv længere' ('You are no longer a werewolf'), the curse is broken forever. The famous Danish ballad 'Liden Kirsten' tells of a werewolf attack outside Vestervig Church in Thy, one of the earliest documented Danish werewolf legends
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Vasuki (King of Serpents)
description: Vasuki is the king of the nagas (serpent beings) in Hindu mythology and one of the most important serpent deities. He is best known for his role in the Samudra Manthana (the churning of the Ocean of Milk), where he served as the churning rope wrapped around Mount Mandara. The devas (gods) held Vasuki's tail while the asuras (demons) held his head, and as they pulled him back and forth, he released a tremendous amount of venom and fire. The poison was so potent it threatened to destroy all creation, forcing Shiva to consume it (turning his throat blue, earning him the name Nilakantha). Vasuki wears the nishagandha jewel on his head and is associated with wealth, protection, and fertility. He is considered a devotee of Shiva, who wears him as an ornament around his neck. In some traditions, Vasuki is one of the eight serpent kings (Ashta Nagas) who rule the underworld realm of Patala
source: Bhagavata Purana, Vishnu Purana, Mahabharata (Adi Parva), Hindu mythology

name: Verdalsdraugen
description: Verdalsdraugen (the Verdal Draug) is a sea draug specific to the Verdal area at the northern end of the Trondheimsfjord. The draug is a malevolent undead being from Norwegian folklore, and the Verdalsdraugen is a localized version haunting the Verdal coast and the lower reaches of the Verdalselva river. According to local tradition, the Verdalsdraugen is the ghost of a drowned fisherman who now appears to warn of approaching storms and shipwrecks. He is most often seen sitting on the rocks at the mouth of the Verdalselva, wearing oilskins and a sou'wester hat, with seaweed hanging from his clothes. If a boat passes too close, the draug will grab its gunwale and try to pull it under. However, if you write your name on a piece of wood and throw it to him, he will release the boat and leave you alone. The Verdalsdraugen is part of the rich coastal folklore of the Trondheimsfjord region
source: Norse mythology; Draugar are undead spirits of the dead, documented in the Sagas and Nordic folklore.

name: Vette
description: Vette (feminine: vetta, plural: vetter, from Old Norse vættr meaning wight/spirit) is a general term in Norwegian folklore for nature spirits and supernatural beings. The vetter are guardian spirits of specific natural places - forests, lakes, rivers, mountains, rocks, and farm buildings. The concept is related to the Old Norse landvættir (land spirits) who protected the land itself. In Norwegian folk belief, every place had its own vette - the skogsvette (forest spirit), vannvette (water spirit), fjellvette (mountain spirit), and husvette (house spirit). Vetter could be benevolent if respected but dangerous if offended. Making offerings at sacred trees, rocks, or waterfalls was a way to maintain good relations with the local vette. The word vette appears in the common phrase vetter og skrømt (spirits and ghosts)
source: Scandinavian folklore; Vættir are nature spirits of the land and water.

name: Vonde-Åsmund
description: Vonde-Åsmund (Evil Åsmund) is the restless ghost of Åsmund Rygnestad (ca. 1540-1596), a historical outlaw from Rygnestad in the Setesdal valley. Åsmund was a violent, law-defying man who fought as a mercenary in the Dutch war for independence and later built the famous Rygnestadloftet as his fortified storehouse — now a protected historic building. After his death, his ghost was said to haunt the Rygnestad area, unable to find peace due to his violent life. Vonde-Åsmund appears as a tall, dark figure at the Rygnestad farm, particularly near the loft he built. He is sometimes seen riding a black horse along the valley road. The legend says his spirit is bound to the treasure he hid somewhere on the farm. Vonde-Åsmund is a historical figure who has become a local folk legend — the line between history and folklore is blurred in his story
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Penyimbang Laut (Water Spirit of Brunei)
description: Penyimbang Laut (Sea Balancer) is a powerful water spirit in Bruneian folklore that governs the rivers, estuaries, and coastal waters of Brunei Darussalam. This ancient spirit is believed to have existed since before the founding of the Brunei Sultanate, dwelling in the deep pools of the Brunei River and along the coast. The spirit is both a guardian of waterways and a judge of human conduct — rewarding those who properly respect the waters with abundant catches and safe passage, while punishing those who pollute, overfish, or show disrespect with storms, boat accidents, and poor fishing. Traditional Bruneian fishermen make offerings of yellow rice, betel nut, and traditional cakes before embarking on voyages. Penyimbang Laut is said to be particularly active during the monsoon transitions, when the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is thinnest
source: https://www.progresif.com/blog/brunei-folklore

name: White Reindeer
description: The White Reindeer is the most sacred animal in Sami belief, a spirit creature associated with the sun goddess Beaivi and the mythic reindeer Meandash. Seeing a white reindeer was considered a powerful omen — an encounter with the divine. Its appearance in dreams or visions signaled major life changes. The white reindeer was the most valuable sacrifice to the gods — white reindeer were specifically offered to Beaivi at the winter solstice to ensure the sun's return, and to Bieggolmmái to control the winds. In Sami shamanism, the reindeer was the most important power animal, used for offerings and depicted on shaman drums. The noaidi would wear a coat made from reindeer fur and antlers in rituals to connect with the great reindeer spirit. All parts of the reindeer had magical properties — its skin, fur, meat, hooves, and especially the antlers, which reached toward the sky and connected earth to the universe. The white reindeer specifically was the purest manifestation of this sacred animal, the closest connection between the human and divine realms
source: laits.utexas.edu; MDPI Religions 2021 (Animals in Saami Shamanism)

name: White Witch of Rose Hall (Annie Palmer)
description: The White Witch of Rose Hall is Jamaica most famous ghost story -- the restless spirit of Annie Palmer, the cruel mistress of Rose Hall Plantation in Montego Bay, who allegedly murdered three husbands and countless enslaved workers through her practice of black magic (obeah). According to legend, Annie Palmer was born in England but raised in Haiti, where she learned voodoo from her Haitian nurse. She came to Jamaica as a young woman and married John Palmer, the wealthy owner of Rose Hall. Dissatisfied with her marriage, she murdered him and then married and killed two more husbands. She also took many enslaved lovers, whose bodies were found in hidden graves across the plantation. Annie was finally killed by an enslaved man named Takoo (or Taku) in revenge for her cruelty. Her ghost is said to haunt the Great House of Rose Hall, appearing as a beautiful woman in a white dress who transforms into a hag, galloping across the plantation on horseback, or wandering the grounds wailing. Visitors to Rose Hall Great House (now a museum) report cold spots, disembodied footsteps, and the sensation of being watched
source: Jamaican oral tradition, Jamaica folklore

name: Yam-Nahar
description: Yam-Nahar (literally 'Sea-River') is the god of the sea and rivers in ancient Syrian (Ugaritic) mythology, the personification of the destructive power of the waters. Known as Prince Yam and Judge Nahar, he is son of the supreme god El and the beloved of his father. Yam is depicted as a serpentine deity, often identified with the sea monster Lotan (Leviathan). In the Baal Cycle, Yam challenges the storm god Baal for kingship of the gods, sending messengers to demand Baal's tribute. Baal defeats Yam in cosmic combat using divine weapons crafted by the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis, establishing order over chaos. This Chaoskampf myth is one of the earliest recorded divine combat narratives and directly influenced the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Hebrew Bible imagery of Yahweh's defeat of Leviathan, and Greek myths of Zeus versus Typhon
source: KTU 1.1-1.6 (Ugaritic Baal Cycle); scholarly works by Mark Smith, Jürg Eggler, John Day

name: Saint Yared
description: Saint Yared is the legendary 6th-century Ethiopian saint who founded the liturgical music tradition of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Born in Axum, Yared was a slow learner as a child who often ran away from his studies. One day, inspired by watching a caterpillar persistently climb a stalk after repeated falls, he returned to his studies with renewed dedication. He was later taken to Heaven where three Holy Spirits taught him the arts of vocal performance, composition, and poetry. He created the five-note scale system (zema) and composed the Deggua (hymn book), inventing musical notation for the Ge'ez language. His music was so beautiful that angels descended from heaven to listen. He served Emperor Gebre Meskel until retiring to the Semien mountains where he is said to have been taken up to heaven without dying
source: Ethiopian Orthodox tradition — Saint Yared is the father of Ethiopian music.

name: Yawm Saub (God of Creation)
description: Yawm Saub (also Yer Shau or simply Saub — 'The One Who Knows Everything') is the high god and creator in Hmong cosmology. He is the supreme celestial being who created the world and all living things, though he is somewhat remote and delegates daily affairs to lesser spirits. Saub is depicted as polygynous, living in a celestial house with a garden and pigs — very human in his nature yet all-seeing and all-knowing. When the evil spirit Ntxwj Nyog began devouring human souls, Saub sent the first shaman Siv Yis to combat him. It was Saub who advised the surviving siblings after the great flood to marry and repopulate the earth, and who told them to carve the resulting mass into twelve pieces that became the Hmong clans. Saub provided the first seeds for agriculture, caused the first hen to lay eggs, and taught humanity proper rituals. Unlike Ntxwj Nyog who is actively involved in causing harm, Saub is benevolent but distant — he set the world in motion and provides shamans with power but rarely intervenes directly
source: Hmong religion — Yawm Saub supreme creator deity of Hmong cosmology.

name: Yocahu (Taino Supreme God of Fertility)
description: Yocahu (Yucahu Bagua Maorocoti) was the supreme deity and masculine spirit of fertility in Taino mythology -- the greatest of all zemis. His full name, recorded by the Spanish missionary Fray Ramon Pane in 1498, carries multiple meanings: Yucahu means giver of cassava (the staple crop), Bagua means master of the sea, and Maorocoti means conceived without male intervention -- born solely from his mother Atabey, the goddess of fresh water. Yocahu is the supreme creator god who shaped the Earth, created the sun and moon from a cave, and molded the first humans from clay. He is the god of agriculture, peace, and tranquility, representing goodness and order in the Taino universe. His throne is atop El Yunque Peak in Puerto Rico El Yunque National Forest -- the tallest mountain in the reserve, perpetually shrouded in cloud (the Taino called it yuke, meaning White Lands). From there, Yocahu battles the destructive goddess Guabancex, shielding his people from hurricanes. He is also known as the Sleeping Giant (El Gigante Dormido), whose reclining form is visible in the mountain profile
source: Taino oral tradition, Puerto Rico folklore

name: Zar
description: Zar spirits are a class of supernatural beings in Eritrean folk belief, particularly among Tigrinya-speaking communities and the broader Horn of Africa region. Unlike the purely malevolent Buda, Zar spirits are ambivalent—they can cause illness and misfortune when angered but may also become protective allies when properly honored through ritual. The Zar possession cult is an important traditional healing system in Eritrea, involving drumming, dancing, and trance ceremonies designed to appease spirits possessing individuals. A person 'ridden' by a Zar spirit may experience physical or mental illness, social withdrawal, or behavioral changes. Diagnosis involves a traditional healer identifying the specific Zar, followed by a ceremony where the spirit is acknowledged, honored, and convinced to reduce its demands. Zar spirits are believed to have distinct personalities, preferences, and demands, often requiring specific colors, perfumes, or foods In Eritrea folklore, this figure is known among the Eritrea people.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C4%81r / https://www.jstor.org/stable/219657

name: Zmey
description: Zmey is a spirit from Bulgaria mythology. In Macedonian tales and folk songs, Zmey are described as extraordinarily intelligent beings with hypnotizing eyes, possessing a human-like form with a snake's tail and golden wings. They live in caves or on remote mountain tops and are extremely wise. The Zmey has a dual nature: they are territorial guardians who protect villages and fight destructive female Lamia in the skies during storms, yet they also fall passionately in love with human women, often kidnapping them to their mountain lairs. A Zmey can shape-shift into smoke, a spark, a firebird, a snake, a cloud, or a handsome man. In Macedonian belief, a woman may conceive a Zmey after a prolonged pregnancy of 15-20 months, and the child is born with small wings under the arms visible only to righteous people. Zmeys battle Lamia in the sky during storms to protect wheat harvests—the Zmey's spirit astrally projects into the clouds while his body sleeps. A crossbreed between a serpent and a samovila may also produce a Zmey
source: Bulgarian folklore — Zmey spirit documented in Bulgarian oral tradition.

name: Zmey
description: The Zmey (Macedonian: Змеј) is a dragon-like creature central to Macedonian folklore, distinct from the purely malevolent dragons of Western tradition.
